page: Amazon Web Services m5.16xlarge is a general-purpose instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor and Intel Xeon 8175M processors. It features 64 vCPUs across 32 physical cores with hyperthreading enabled at a base clock speed of 3.1 GHz. The instance configuration provides 256 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, maintaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio. It includes a 20 Gbps baseline network bandwidth, operates without bundled local instance storage, and contains zero discrete GPUs.

Benchmark evaluation shows distinct performance characteristics between single-threaded execution and parallel compute. Single-core benchmarks, including Geekbench (1039.0) and stress-ng (1286.19), score in the lower 25% of measured cloud hardware. In contrast, multi-threaded execution scales across all 64 vCPUs to achieve average results in PassMark CPU (43191.13), multi-core stress-ng (54159.82), and Clang software compilation. Uncached memory read bandwidth is a highlight, reaching 192.72 GB/sec for large blocks, ranking in the top quartile.

From a resource utilization perspective, the instance offers balanced density for applications that do not require GPU acceleration or ephemeral local disks. Persistent storage requirements must be met using external network-attached volumes. The hardware configuration and benchmark profiles align with multi-threaded enterprise services, distributed caching systems like Redis, static web serving fleets, and mid-tier relational database backends.
description: Amazon Web Services m5.16xlarge is a general-purpose virtual instance based on the AWS Nitro hypervisor and x86_64 architecture. Powered by Intel Xeon 8175M processors running at 3.1 GHz, it offers 64 vCPUs across 32 physical cores alongside 256 GB of DDR4 RAM, resulting in a standard 1:4 core-to-memory allocation. The instance features 20 Gbps baseline network bandwidth, contains no integrated GPUs, and includes no local instance storage. Benchmark results show average multi-core processing power and database transaction speeds, balanced by upper-quartile large-block read memory bandwidth reaching 192.72 GB/sec. However, single-core CPU throughput registers in the lower quartile across tests like Geekbench and stress-ng. This instance provides a cost-efficient resource density for horizontally threaded enterprise workloads, mid-tier data stores, in-memory caching systems, and high-volume web serving fleets.
